bib.title: Unifying the Perspectives of NLP and Software Engineering: A Survey on Language Models for Code

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Unifying the Perspectives of NLP and Software Engineering: A Survey on Language Models for Code", Ziyin Zhang, Chaoyu Chen, Bingchang Liu, Cong Liao, Zi Gong, Hang Yu, Jianguo Li, Rui Wang (Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ. / Ant Group). arXiv 2311.07989v7 [cs.CL], 26 Jun 2024. Header says preprint; the text uses an ICLR/TMLR-style template with no venue named. Living list at github.com/codefuse-ai/Awesome-Code-LLM.

COVERAGE: 125 pages, 486,901 chars extracted. Read in full: abstract, intro, Sec 2.1.5-2.4, Sec 3-8 (body ends at about p.31), Appendix A tables 5-6 and 10 and Appendix B tables 11-18. Only skimmed: 2.1.1 beginning (requirements and UI/UX taxonomy lists), and the rest of the taxonomy citation lists in 2.1.2-2.1.4 and Fig 3-7 (lines 330-1135, pages ~5-12), plus Appendix A tables 7-9. These are citation lists, not results. References (~pp.31-115) skimmed only for structure. Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: Code pretraining corpora differ widely in size. CodeSearchNet 20 GB, The Pile code 95 GB, ROOTS code 163 GB, CodeParrot 1 TB, The Stack 3,136 GB, The Stack v2 32 TB.
  number: see row list
  setup: Table 2, size in GB, files in millions, number of languages. Pile and ROOTS rows count only the code part.
  quote: "CodeSearchNeta 20 6.5 6 / The Pilebc 95 19 - / CodeParrotd 1K 115 30 / The Stacke 3136 317 30 / ROOTSf 163 15 13 / The Stack v2g 32K 3K 619"
  where: p.20 (~line 1581)
  caveat: the prose says CodeParrot is "50GB" and the Stack "3TB", while the table says CodeParrot "1K" GB. Internal inconsistency, flag it.

- claim: General pretraining mixes already contain a lot of code. Pile has 95 GB code of 800 GB; ROOTS has 163 GB over 13 languages of 1.6 TB; LLaMA's data has 328 GB of GitHub code; LaMDA is 12.5% code and PaLM 5%.
  number: 95/800 GB; 163 GB/1.6 TB; 328 GB; 12.5%; 5%
  setup: figures as reported by the survey, citing each model's paper.
  quote: "The Pile (Gao et al., 2021), for example, includes 95GB of code crawled from GitHub out of its 800GB raw dataset, while the multilingual pretraining dataset ROOTS (Laurençon et al., 2022) also contains 163GB of code spanning 13 programming languages in its 1.6TB compound." and "LaMDA (Thoppilan et al., 2022) and PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2023), whose pre-training dataset contains 12.5% and 5% code respectively, achieve 14.0 and 26.2 pass@1 performance on HumanEval"
  where: p.19

- claim: Additional (continual) pretraining on code lifts HumanEval a lot. Codex is GPT-3 plus 100B code tokens. PaLM-Coder adds 7.8B code tokens. Code LLaMA adds over 500B code tokens to LLaMA 2.
  number: 100B; 7.8B; >500B tokens
  setup: HumanEval 0-shot pass@1, Table 1. LLaMA 2 70B 29.9, Code LLaMA-Python 34B 53.7, PaLM 540B 26.2 vs PaLM-Coder 540B 36.0, Codex 12B 28.8, GPT-J 6B 11.6.
  quote: "Codex, which are GPT-3 checkpoints pretrained on 100B additional code tokens"; "Chowdhery et al. (2023) train PaLM on 7.8B additional code tokens to obtain PaLM-Coder"; "Rozière et al. (2023) train LLaMA 2 (Touvron et al., 2023b) on more than 500B code tokens to acquire Code LLaMA"
  where: p.20
  note: the survey calls this "extra/additional/continual pretraining" and says it is still self-supervised, not finetuning (footnote 6, p.18).

- claim: Table 1 gives a checkable HumanEval/MBPP table for general LMs.
  number: pass@1 HumanEval (MBPP): LLaMA 65B 23.7 (37.7); LLaMA 2 70B 29.9 (45.0); GPT-NeoX 20B 15.4; BLOOM 176B 15.5; LaMDA 137B 14.0 (14.8); PaLM 540B 26.2 (36.8); Phi-1.5 1.3B 41.4 (43.5); Baichuan 2 13B 17.1 (30.2); Qwen 14B 32.3 (40.8); Mistral 7B 30.5 (47.5); DeepSeek 67B 42.7 (57.4); Mixtral 8x7B 40.2 (60.7); DeepSeekMoE 16B 26.8 (39.2); GPT-4 67.0; Gemini Ultra 74.7; Code LLaMA 34B 53.7 (56.2); PaLM 2-S* 37.6 (50.0); Code-Qwen 14B 45.1 (51.4). Pass@100 on HumanEval: LLaMA 79.3, LLaMA 2 89.0, Code LLaMA 94.7.
  setup: HumanEval 0-shot, MBPP 3-shot. Numbers are collected from each model's paper, so they are not run under a common harness. Phi-1.5 is the web variant, Code LLaMA is the Python variant. A few cells (Phi-1.5 and Baichuan 2 MBPP columns) are hard to align in the extraction.
  quote: "LLaMA5 65B 23.7 79.3 37.7 76.8 / GPT-4 67.0 / LLaMA 28 70B 29.9 89.0 45.0 81.5 / Phi-1.59 1.3B 41.4 43.5 ... Code LLaMA18 34B 53.7 94.7 56.2"
  where: Table 1, p.19

- claim: Table 4 (pass@1) compares specialized code models, instruction-finetuned models and the best general LMs.
  number: HumanEval (MBPP). Pretrained: PolyCoder 2.7B 5.6; CodeGen-Mono 16.1B 29.3 (35.3); InCoder 6.7B 15.2 (19.4); SantaCoder 1.1B 14.0 (35.0); CodeGeeX 13B 22.9 (24.4); StarCoder 15.5B 33.6 (52.7); CodeT5+ 16B 30.9; Phi-1 1.3B 50.6 (55.5); DeepSeek Coder 33B 56.1 (66.0). Instruction-tuned: InstructCodeT5+ 16B 35.0; WizardCoder 15.5B 57.3 (51.8); Pangu-Coder 2 15.5B 61.6; OctoCoder 15.5B 46.2; CodeFuse 34B 74.4; DeepSeek Coder-Instruct 33B 79.3 (70.0).
  setup: numbers from the original papers, so prompts and settings may differ.
  quote: "StarCoder 15.5B 33.6 52.7 / Phi-1 1.3B 50.6 55.5 / DeepSeek Coder 33B 56.1 66.0 ... WizardCoder 15.5B 57.3 51.8 / Pangu-Coder 2 15.5B 61.6 - / OctoCoder 15.5B 46.2 - / CodeFuse 34B 74.4 - / DeepSeek Coder-Instruct 33B 79.3 70.0"
  where: Table 4, p.24

- claim: Small models trained on curated or synthetic data match much larger ones. Phi-1 (1.3B) was trained on 7B tokens (6B filtered StackOverflow-type data plus 1B ChatGPT-synthetic). Phi-1.5 used 21B synthetic textbook tokens plus 100B filtered web tokens.
  number: 7B tokens; 6B + 1B; 21B + 100B; 50.6 and 55.5 pass@1; 41.4
  setup: HumanEval and MBPP pass@1. Survey says this is "comparable to" Code LLaMA or PaLM 2. Table 3 lists Phi-1 as 1.3B, 53B tokens seen, 1 language.
  quote: "Phi-1, a 1.3B small model trained on a dataset of only 7B tokens consisting of 6B tokens from StackOverflow and 1B synthetic data generated by ChatGPT but achieving 50.6 pass@1 on HumanEval and 55.5 pass@1 on MBPP"; "Phi-1.5, is trained on 21B tokens of textbook data generated by ChatGPT, and 100B tokens of filtered web data from Stack Overflow and Refined Web (Penedo et al., 2023), and attains 41.4 pass@1 performance on HumanEval."
  where: p.19, p.24; also Sec 5.1 "synthesize 1B tokens of Python textbooks and coding exercises" (p.21)

- claim: Smaller models are trained on more tokens, following the revised scaling law. Baichuan 2 is 13B on 2.6T tokens and Qwen is 14B on 3T.
  number: 2.6T; 3T; HumanEval 17.1 and 32.3
  setup: pass@1 HumanEval 0-shot.
  quote: "Baichuan 2 (Yang et al., 2023a), for example, is a 13B model trained on 2.6T tokens, while Qwen (Bai et al., 2023) is a 14B model trained on 3T tokens. They achieve 17.1 and 32.3 pass@1 on HumanEval, respectively."
  where: p.19

- claim: A mixture-of-experts model reaches or passes larger dense models with fewer active parameters.
  number: Mixtral 8x7B, 13B active, 40.2; DeepSeekMoE 16B, 2.8B active, 26.8
  setup: HumanEval pass@1.
  quote: "Mixtral 8x7B, where only 13B parameters are activated for each token during inference, but achieving 40.2 on HumanEval and surpassing much larger dense models such as LLaMA 2."
  where: p.19

- claim: Objective taxonomy. Causal LM (next-token, decoder), masked LM (about 15% of tokens masked, so inefficient), ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (loss on all tokens), T5 span corruption with sentinels, prefix LM, UL2 mixed denoisers. Code adds identifier tagging, masked identifier prediction, deobfuscation, naturalization, AST/data-flow edge prediction, contrastive learning, and text-code and code-text generation.
  number: 15%
  setup: conceptual, Sec 3.1-3.4 and 5.2-5.3. Equations (3), (4) and (5) give CLM, MLM and seq2seq.
  quote: "it suffers from low training efficiency, since only a small set of tokens (usually 15%) are masked (and thus “trained on”)"; "Tay et al. (2023b) argue that span corruption is also closely related to CLM, since one can mask out the whole input text as a single span and train the decoder to generate it autoregressively."
  where: p.16-17

- claim: UL2 finding. At equal compute, encoder-decoder models do better than decoder-only ones. The survey says other works agree. Decoder-only models still dominate.
  number: none
  setup: reported by the survey from Tay et al. 2023b, Wang et al. 2022c and Soltan et al. 2022. The survey ran no experiment.
  quote: "they find that encoder-decoder models perform better under the same computation budget constraint. Other researches have also found that such encoder-decoder models generally perform better than causal decoder-only models"
  where: p.17

- claim: Fill-in-the-middle (FIM), also called causal masking, is span corruption adapted to decoder-only models. It lets a model fill blanks, and FIM models score higher than CLM-only CodeGen in Table 4, but the survey says the benefit is "controversial".
  number: none
  setup: InCoder, SantaCoder, StarCoder, DeepSeek Coder and CodeShell use FIM. Confounded by model size and data.
  quote: "these objectives also lead to higher performance on downstream tasks when compared with CLM-only models such as CodeGen, although the exact benefits of infilling training remain controversial (Nijkamp et al., 2023a)."
  where: p.25
  also: PanGu-Coder found MLM and masked CLM underperform CLM-only in a decoder.

- claim: Table 3 lists the training details of each code LM. Examples: CodeGen-Multi (Mono) 350M-16.1B, 1.6TB (1.8TB) data, 1T (1.2T) tokens seen; StarCoder 15.5B, 8192 context, 815 GB, 1T tokens, 86 languages, MQA, FIM; SantaCoder 1.1B, 268 GB, 236B tokens, FIM; PolyCoder 160M-2.7B, 254 GB, 39B tokens, 12 languages; CodeBERT 125M, 20 GB, 105B tokens; AlphaCode 300M-41B, 715 GB, 967B tokens, 13 languages; CodeGeeX 13B, 850B tokens, 23 languages; CuBERT 350M, 93B tokens seen.
  number: see list
  setup: Table 3 covers architecture, size, vocab, context, position embedding, precision, attention, init, objectives, dataset size, tokens seen, number of languages. It excludes the tokens used to train the initialisation model.
  quote: "2023-05 StarCoder GPT-2 15.5B 49K 8192 absolute fp32 MQA ! ! - FIM 815GB 1T 86 BigCode"; "2022-03 CodeGen-Multi(Mono) GPT-J 350M-16.1B 50K 2048 RoPE fp16 MHA ! ! - CLM 1.6TB(1.8TB)/506B(577B) 1T(1.2T) 6(1)"
  where: Table 3, p.22

- claim: Code data has built-in structure. CodeSearchNet has 6.5M functions, 2.3M paired with docs. Commit histories can be instructions: CommitPackFT is 2 GB and 742K samples. Star count may be a poor quality filter.
  number: 6.5M; 2.3M; 2GB; 742K
  setup: Sec 5.1.
  quote: "of the 6.5M functions in CodeSearchNet, 2.3M are paired with natural language documentation"; "construct a 2GB dataset CommitPackFT containing 742K samples of instruction data for code"; "Allal et al. (2023) suggest that star count correlates poorly with downstream performance"
  where: p.20-21

- claim: Instruction tuning for code, with sizes. InstructCodeT5+ uses 20K InstructGPT-generated samples. WizardCoder evolves 20K Code Alpaca samples into 78K (Evol-Instruct) to finetune StarCoder. Pangu-Coder 2 builds 68K from 20K and adds RRTF reinforcement learning. OctoCoder uses git commits. CodeFuse uses multi-task finetuning (MFT) on Code LLaMA, reaching 74.4 pass@1.
  number: 20K; 78K; 68K; 74.4
  setup: HumanEval pass@1. The survey says 74.4 surpasses GPT-4's published 67.0.
  quote: "WizardCoder (Luo et al., 2023) follows the methods of WizardLM (Xu et al., 2024) to evolve 20K code Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023) samples into a 78K dataset and uses it to finetune StarCoder."; "CodeFuse-CodeLLaMA, achieving 74.4 pass@1 on HumanEval and surpassing even the performance of GPT-4 published in OpenAI (2023)."
  where: p.20, p.25

- claim: RL for code gets automatic reward from compilers and unit tests. CodeRL uses four reward levels (compile error, runtime error, unit-test failure, pass) plus a token-level critic and REINFORCE. PPOCoder, CompCoder and RLTF use PPO or finer error feedback.
  number: 4 reward levels
  setup: descriptive.
  quote: "CodeRL (Le et al., 2022) is one such model, which defines four levels of rewards for each generated program (viz. compile error, runtime error, unit test failure, pass)"
  where: p.26

- claim: Metrics move from content overlap (BLEU, CodeBLEU, exact match) to functional correctness, pass@k (Kulal 2019, Chen 2021) and pass n@k (AlphaCode).
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.2.
  quote: "pass@k, proposed by Kulal et al. (2019) and refined by Chen et al. (2021b), which is an unbiased estimator of the model’s chance in passing all unit tests of a program with any of k generated samples."
  where: p.14

- claim: HumanEval is saturated and unrepresentative. Repository-level SWE-bench was far lower. HumanEval has 164 problems, MBPP 974, SWE-bench 2,294.
  number: 12.5%; 164; 974; 2294
  setup: SWE-agent result on SWE-bench as cited from Yang et al. 2024b. The sizes come from Tables 6 and 10.
  quote: "with the most recent SWE-agent resolving only 12.5% real-world GitHub issues in SWE-bench (Yang et al., 2024b)"; "its scoreboard has been manipulated to near perfect"; "2021-07 HumanEval Chen et al. (2021b) 164 Python"; "2023-10 SWE-Bench Jimenez et al. (2023) 2294 Python"
  where: p.29-30; Tables 6 and 10 (p.117, p.121)

- claim: Appendix B benchmark results exist for non-generation tasks. CRUXEval pass@1 input/output: GPT-4o+CoT 77.4/88.7; Claude-3-Opus+CoT 73.4/82.0; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 (236B, 21B active)+CoT 70.0/75.1; CodeLLaMA 34B 46.5/41.1; Phi-1 13.9/23.3. NL-code search MRR average: CoCoSoDa 78.8; CodeRetriever 77.4; CodeT5+large 77.4; CodeBERT 69.3. Translation pass@1: GPT-3.5 self-debug 89.1 (92.7). Defect detection Devign: CodeT5base 65.8 finetuned vs WizardCoder 15B 54.4 0-shot.
  number: see list
  setup: Tables 11-18, numbers collected from different papers and splits, with differing implementations noted in the Table 12 caption.
  quote: "GPT-4o + CoT - 77.4 88.7"; "CoCoSoDa 81.8 76.4 92.1 75.7 76.3 70.3 78.8"; "CodeT5base 65.8 ! ! - Wang et al. (2021f)"
  where: pp.122-125

- claim: The survey's scope is large and there is a historical arc.
  number: 70+ models, 40+ tasks, 180+ datasets, 900 related works
  setup: abstract. Code modelling went from statistical models and RNNs to pretrained Transformers and LLMs, the same path as NLP.
  quote: "covering 70+ models, 40+ evaluation tasks, 180+ datasets, and 900 related works"
  where: abstract, p.1

- claim: Architecture timeline for implementation choices (pre-norm from GPT-2, parallel attention from GPT-J, RoPE and ALiBi, MQA and GQA, FlashAttention, FP16 to BF16). Code decoders follow NLP practice: pre-norm everywhere, RoPE/MQA/parallel attention adopted by several, FlashAttention in the three latest (StarCoder, Phi-1, CodeFuse).
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.5 and 4.2, Fig 9.
  quote: "BF16 has now become more popular (Chowdhery et al., 2023; Scao et al., 2022), as it can represent the same range of floating point numbers as FP32, thus preventing numerical overflowing and underflowing during training."
  where: p.17-18

- claim: Small diffusion model for code.
  number: 75M
  setup: CodeFusion (Singh et al. 2023) on three code synthesis datasets, as reported by the survey.
  quote: "a 75M diffusion model can outperform StarCoder, CodeT5+, and GPT-3 on three code synthesis datasets"
  where: p.25

LIMITS
- It is a survey, so no new experiments. All numbers are copied from original papers under different prompts and settings. It states "we use self-reported number whenever available" for dataset sizes. Tables 1 and 4 mix 0-shot, 3-shot and different harnesses, so rankings between rows are weak evidence.
- Data cutoffs: Table 1 reaches Mixtral, Gemini Ultra and DeepSeek around early 2024. The survey admits HumanEval is near saturated. It does not cover post-2024 models except Tables 17 and 18.
- Its own concessions: "whether or not this architecture [UniLM] is suitable for code processing is yet to be explored at scale"; the benefit of FIM is controversial; the effects of training on AI-generated data are "yet to be investigated at scale"; decoder-only models have not been augmented with code-specific auxiliary objectives; data/control flow has not been used at scale; code-specific features (AST, DFG) mostly appear in encoder and encoder-decoder models.
- Internal inconsistencies: Sec 5.1 prose gives CodeParrot as 50GB, while Table 2 says 1K GB. Two different GPT-4 numbers (67.0 and early 82) are both quoted.
- No scaling-law experiments, no ablations on data mix, and no direct comparison of objectives under controlled conditions.

BUILDS ON (as printed): Vaswani et al. 2017; Devlin et al. 2019 (BERT); Radford et al. 2018/2019; Brown et al. 2020 (GPT-3); Raffel et al. 2020 (T5); Lewis et al. 2020 (BART); Clark et al. 2020 (ELECTRA); Tay et al. 2023b (UL2); Chen et al. 2021b (Codex, HumanEval); Austin et al. 2021 (MBPP); Hoffmann et al. 2022 (revised scaling law); Kaplan et al. 2020; Lu et al. 2021 (CodeXGLUE); Gao et al. 2021 (Pile); Kocetkov et al. 2023 (The Stack); Husain et al. 2019 (CodeSearchNet); Gunasekar et al. 2023 (Phi-1); Li et al. 2023i (Phi-1.5); Rozière et al. 2023 (Code LLaMA); Muennighoff et al. 2024 (OctoPack); Luo et al. 2023 (WizardCoder); Ouyang et al. 2022 (InstructGPT); Wei et al. 2022b, Sanh et al. 2022, Chung et al. 2022 (instruction tuning). Concurrent surveys: Hou et al. 2023, Zheng et al. 2023b, She et al. 2023, Zan et al. 2023.

CODE: none. Equations only: (3) P(x)=prod p_theta(x_i | x_1:i-1); (4) MLM max prod_{m in M} p(m | x_hat); (5) p(y|x_hat)=prod p(y_i | x_hat, y_1:i-1) with <extra_id_i> sentinels. Transformer block post-norm (6)-(7), pre-norm (8)-(9), GPT-J parallel (10).

FIGURES (not rendered; captions from the text only, figures.py not run)
- Fig 1 (p.3), taxonomy of code LMs: raw LM, adapted LM, specialized (encoder, decoder CLM/FIM, UniLM, encoder-decoder), instruction finetuning, RL. Useful as a model-zoo map for note 03.
- Fig 2 (p.4), timeline of HumanEval pass@1 2021-2024 (GPT-J 6B to DeepSeek Coder 33B, CodeFuse 33B). Shows how fast code ability climbed. The data points are plotted but not given as numbers.
- Fig 9 (p.17), implementation changes in LLMs (block architecture, position embeddings, attention optimisation, mixed precision).
- Figs 3-8, taxonomy lists of tasks, not useful for the notes.

- Table text extraction loses column alignment where cells are blank (Table 1 MBPP and pass@100 columns for Phi-1.5, Baichuan 2, Qwen, Mistral, Mixtral and others, and Table 4). The values quoted above were checked against the prose where possible. Verify cell positions against the PDF page before citing a cell.
- Sections 2.1.1-2.1.4 and Appendix A tables 7-9 not read in detail (listed above). The reference list was skimmed only.
